label: No Call to Mrs. King
detail: The Democratic nominee stays silent after Martin Luther King Jr.'s October 1960 arrest and makes no sympathetic call to his wife.
assumption: Black voters, especially in northern cities and border states, get no signal of the nominee's concern and so shift somewhat toward the other major party or stay home, while white Southern reaction is unchanged.
facts_text: A Black minister and civil rights leader was arrested in Atlanta in October 1960 and sentenced to months of hard labor in a Georgia state prison.
Black newspapers and ministers have asked both major candidates to speak out.
nominee_news: He has made no public statement on the jailing of a prominent Black minister in Georgia, and he has not been in contact with the minister's family.
Civil rights leaders have noted his silence while the minister remains in a Georgia jail.
research_questions: How much did Black voters' support for the Democratic ticket change between 1956 and 1960 in northern cities?
How widely did Black voters learn of the phone call and the related intervention before election day?
Did Black turnout in Illinois, Michigan and other close states rise or fall in 1960 compared with 1956?
How did Black voters respond in past elections when a candidate stayed silent on a civil rights crisis?
source_text: John F. Kennedy does not call Coretta Scott King after Martin Luther King Jr.'s October 1960 arrest.
